text: Chapter 2 spent real time on Update Sets: capturing changes, previewing and committing them, and resolving collisions at scale. None of that work goes away — Update Sets remain how most ServiceNow configuration still moves between instances today. But as an application and its team grow, Update Sets alone stop being enough.

An Update Set is a point-in-time snapshot. It tells you what changed between opening it and closing it. It doesn't tell you who changed one specific line two years ago, why they changed it, what earlier versions looked like, or let two developers safely work on the same file at once without colliding. That's not a flaw in Update Sets — it's simply outside what they were built to do.

For scoped applications built in Studio, ServiceNow provides real, native Source Control Integration: connecting the application's actual files to an external Git repository, like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. Once connected, the code lives in a real Git repository the same way any other software project's code does, instead of depending solely on Update Sets to carry it between instances.

That brings in the same practices general software development already relies on. Meaningful diffs show exactly which lines changed. Blame and history track who changed a file, and when, as far back as the repository goes. Branching lets multiple developers work on separate features without colliding. And pull-request-style review means changes get approved before they're merged — a real code-review gate an Update Set, on its own, doesn't naturally provide.

This matters for where the course is headed. Chapter 4 covers the Automated Test Framework, and Chapter 5 covers CI/CD concepts — both assume code that can be versioned, branched, and tested in a pipeline. Source control integration is what makes a scoped application's code look that way in the first place: not configuration that only lives inside one instance, but code that lives in a repository, ready for an automated pipeline to work against. Next: the real, conceptual steps for connecting an application to a Git repository.
